projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Margaret Amick was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: This interview is with Mary Margaret Amick, spelled A-M-I-C-K, Margaret was born on July 3, 1926 during WWII she served as a civilian working for the Arthur Hurt Machine Shop which made parts for the Boeing Aircraft Company. This interview is taking place on August 6, 2013 at [redacted] in Castle Rock, Colorado where Margaret currently resides. The interviewer is Larry Adams, a Veteran’s History Project volunteer for the Douglas County History Research Center at the Phillip S. Miller Library in Castle Rock, Colorado. Margaret’s son David Amick is also present during the interview. The interview is being conducted for the Veteran’s History Project at the Library of Congress. So let’s start with a little background information, Margaret, when and where were you born?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I was born in Denver, Colorado, ah, 1926.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Were you born at home or in a hospital?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: At home.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Yeah, I guess that was customary in those days.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: It was customary then, right.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What were the names of your parents?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Harold A. Bradley and Helen M. Bradley.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What were their occupations?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And my dad worked for ACME, ah, ACME Fast Freight.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And, my mother was just a home maker.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did your dad drive the freight trucks or did he work at the, did your dad?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, he worked at the, at the, what they called the docks.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay where they brought in and shipped out various things.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Okay, I had three (3) brothers, three (3) brothers?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What were their names?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, four (4) brothers [laughter] and three (3) sisters.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Oh, four (4) brothers and three (3) sisters?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And three (3) sisters.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What are your brother’s names?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My brother’s name was Hal was the oldest, than Bob John, who passed away, and Dick.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And, Dick. What about the names of your sisters?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My sisters were Ruth and Dottie.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Wow that was quite a family.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Uh-huh, really.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Eight (8) of you in all.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Seven (7).

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Three (3) sisters and four (4) sons, brothers plus you that makes eight (8) in your family.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, what am I sayin’ wrong? I have two (2) sisters, two (2) sisters.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, two (2) sisters. Okay, two (2) sisters, right, so there were seven (7) in your family. What about grand-parents, I noticed in your memoirs, you talk about your grandmother, Nana.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My Grandma Nana lived us off and on.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was she on your mother’s side or your dad’s side?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And, she was on my mother’s side.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Can you tell us a little bit about your grandmother because you talked about her a lot in your memoirs. She’s an important person in your life.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My grandmother was the best grandma there ever was, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: She took us everywhere and did everything with us, she, ah -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Nana was, I think, she was, ah, had her own car and we went up and picked peaches and we did, we did everything.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What was it like growing up in Denver; let’s talk about your elementary school, where was the elementary school located?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My elementary school was, ah, I can’t think of the name of the elementary school, Barnum, no, I didn’t go to Barnum, went to Lincoln.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Oh, Lincoln, that’s right in your memoirs, I remember Lincoln.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Lincoln, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you go through grades one (1) through six (6) at Lincoln?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Lincoln one (1) through six (6) and then junior high was, ah, Byers Junior High.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And, I noticed you graduated at age 16 (sixteen), did you skip any grades?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I skipped one (1) grade.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: In elementary school?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, in elementary school.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was that customary in those days to advance students, to skip a grade, did you have to take a test to skip a grade?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: You know, I don’t remember doing that but maybe, I don’t remember doin’ that. But I remember I skipped a grade because I -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You did graduate early.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, I graduated.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you like school, elementary school?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, I loved school.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, did you have some favorite teachers?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: An art teacher was Nicetrom [sp?], she was great. The, ah, English teacher I didn’t like at all, and of course, at that time they would, you didn’t step on the grass and you didn’t chew gum and you couldn’t do a lot of those things. Ah, chewing gum was one thing that I did one time and my teacher, Mrs. Putnam [sp?] put my under her desk [laughter] I’ll never forget it. I set under her desk because I chewed gum. [laughter]

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you have, you walked to school in those days?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I only walked to school.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: How far did you have to walk to school?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh my goodness, ah, elementary school probably about 6 (six) blocks.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, that wasn’t too bad.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And it wasn’t too bad.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about activities outside of school, holidays, what were some of your favorite holidays and how did you celebrate the holidays when you were a young child like that?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We always had a big doings at Christmas time and I always remember my dad with his rolled-up cigar, you know how they used to roll them up. And he’d sit there and smoke that cigar [laughter] my dad would. My mom did nothing but cook, boy she did a lot of cooking and she could cook!

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about some of the other holidays, like 4th of July?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, 4th of July we would buy firecrackers, daddy would go to the store and he’d buy all these firecrackers in a box and we’d set off. We went to Denver Country Club and they had fireworks there that were oh, fabulous. Denver Country Club was Speer Blvd and, where was it, University, I believe at that time. And, we’d always go there and celebrate 4th of July and the fireworks.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about Halloween?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And Halloween, yeah, we would go, we would go along, ah, oh, gosh what was that street, ah isn’t that funny I can’t remember the street.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: For trick or treating?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: For trick or treating and we always went to these well-to-do houses and I can remember they had, ah, a whole box of things in the front and you could take, you could take, ah, big candy bars or you could take, they had all these things that you could take and they were the well-to-do in that, now where was it? It was down, ah, 6th Avenue, seemed to me it was 6th Avenue. I don’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: That’s okay. What about some of the other things you did, you mentioned camping trips, horseback riding, car trips with your grandmother?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, car trips with my grandma, of course, she always took us, I’ll never forget one time she took us up to Grand Junction to help a friend pick peaches. And if you’ve ever picked peaches, you have that fuzz all over you, it was terrible, terrible, but we was helpin’ this friend pick these peaches and my brother, Hal, and who else went Hal and my brother Hal and my brother I don’t remember Bob doin’ that. I don’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, well let’s move on to your middle school, what was it called, junior high?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Byers, Byers Junior High.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Byers Junior High?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And, was that within walking distance, too?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, yeah, it was walkin’ distance [laughter] it was a long way but -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You didn’t take the bus?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, did you like junior high school?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was that fun?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I liked junior high.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, by that time you were in ah, you had skipped a grade, I guess.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I had skipped a grade.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You were younger than most of the students in your -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I was.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you notice that or did it matter?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, it was, ah, it was whole, it wasn’t a whole grade that you skipped, you skipped a half grade so it was let me see, how did we do that? I do know that when I went to high school which was South High School I went to because all my family went to South High School. South High School was at, ah, University, I used to remember those streets so well and I don’t remember 'um now. South High?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: That’s okay, now, around that time, I think the depression was happening in this country, do you remember anything about the depression years?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, I don’t remember that, ah, all I remember is that, ah, rationing, they did a lot of rationing of, ah, meat, ah -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was that during the depression or during the war that came later.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, well that must have been -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: That was the war, you didn’t do any -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Not the depression, I don’t think I remember any of that.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, you don’t remember the depression, yeah, okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Because I was pretty young then.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And your dad was still working, he didn’t lose his job during the depression years?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay so the depression didn’t really affect you. Okay let’s go to the high school years, this was South High School.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What were your favorite subjects in high school?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: You know; I don’t know that I had any favorites other than math, I loved my math, I always liked math. Ah,

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But I understand, I thought I understood that they didn’t let you take math because you were a girl, is that right?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh no! They let you take math.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay they let you take math?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: They let you take math.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you take science courses?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And, some science though I didn’t particularly like science.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You didn’t like science?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Maybe I didn’t like the teacher or something.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay that often matters, yeah.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Then, then, in high school I went to what they called Opportunity School at that time and it was at on 14th Street.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was that Emily Griffith School, Emily Griffith Opportunity School?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: It must have been, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Let’s understand, you went to South High School?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: But then I went to the Emily Griffith during school year because I was taking welding.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, so you went to two (2) schools?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, actually, and I was taking welding and what else did I take there isn’t that funny?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Why did you take welding, it’s not common for a girl to -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I know it isn’t, I know it isn’t.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Why did you take it?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: But it was during the war.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And, so you did anything like that that you could better yourself during the war.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you were preparing for graduations to become a welder, was it necessary to -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Not necessarily to become a welder but become, what they called at the machine shop, was ah, spot welding. Ah, I did some, I can remember welding, I did some welding but, ah -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: At, at Emily Griffith?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: At Emily Griffith, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Yeah, that was before you worked for the Hurt Company back -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You probably valued you because you knew how to weld.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: That’s it, they did and that’s why they hired me, I think in the first place.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, before, go ahead.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I was only sixteen (16) at the time and he wouldn’t, he couldn’t let me do some of the things on the machines and so-forth until I got, what eighteen (18), no sixteen (16) you had to be at least seventeen (17) I think before you could do some of those things.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, okay before you graduate from high school, let’s talk a little bit about some of the fun things you did while you were in high school, did you go to the movies?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We went to the movies on South Broadway and Weber Theater and, also, and Mayan Theater was both on South Broadway in about the 200 block and Mayan was First Avenue, I think. And, ah, I remember my brother won a bicycle and we all thought that was great except they didn’t let us ride, the girls couldn’t ride the bicycle, just the boys.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What was, what was the other theater you mentioned, you mentioned the Mayan, what was the other theater?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Mayan [pronounced "may on"] and Weber.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Weber?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Weber, un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, and, ah, you mentioned in your memoirs that you used to distribute movie theater flyers around the neighborhood.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: That’s what we did to be able to go to the movies, we would deliver these flyers that they had and we’d run up and down, up and down the block, ah, from Alameda to 1st Avenue and deliver these flyers, I’ll never forget that. And, then we’d get a ticket, a free ticket to the theater for something, you know, for a movie.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, didn’t you also win prizes, you mentioned in your memoirs you had a what, a Shirley Temple Doll?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I won a Shirley Temple Doll at one of the theaters, they always gave away prizes at the theater and I won a Shirley Temple Doll once that I dearly loved and I don’t even remember what happened to that Shirley Temple Doll. But then, my brother won ah, bicycle, which of course to us kids, we were poor. We weren’t very wealthy, I’ll tell you and he won this bicycle.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you, also, win tap dancing lessons?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And I worked, yeah, and I can still do them, I think.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You can still tap dance?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, [laughter] I think I could ah, ah, "Roll Out the Barrel" I used to do that "Rollin’ Out the Barrel" and what was some of the other things we did? No I don’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, so now you’ve graduated from high school, you were sixteen (16) graduation was in what year, 1942?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was it ’43?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: I was looking at the "bio", okay, ’43. And, again, you skipped a grade that’s why you were able to graduate -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: When you, at a younger age. And, so the war was going on and you’ve already been trained in welding and now you’re going to work at Arthur Hart, Arthur Hurt?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Hurt.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, did you start right away after you graduated?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Wasn’t long after I graduated that I started and, of course, Hurt and Company was just a half a block away from where I lived.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Oh, really.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, on, it was on Kalamath Street and, ah, let’s see I lived at 283 South Kalamath Street and, and the Hurt and Company was at 218, I think, South Kalamath Street? Yeah, ah, and I started there.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What did you start doing, were you welding right away or did you have to wait until you were eighteen (18) to do welding?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I couldn’t weld, I didn’t weld but I did run, ah, lathes, drill presses, spot welding, spot welding I did do. 'Cause we worked, ah, for things for Boeing Aircraft so we did a lot of, ah, a lot of things.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Do you know what parts you made for the Boeing Aircraft Company; did you make parts for the B-17 Flying Fortress?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: For the B-17 and I, I worked on, ah, drill, not a drill, it was, ah, it was, ah, gosh what were they called? They were bolts and they were five (5) they were very precise silver, I’ll never forget that, silver, ah, on these bolts just about, ah, about a half inch or, of the silver and it was, you what did you do? You, ah, I can’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Do you know what, how they were used on the B-17?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And I don’t have it.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: The wings or the tail, you don’t have it?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I don’t have any idea.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I do know that Art Hurt knew a lot of the Boeing Aircraft people would come in and, I’ll never forget, Nitta Downing, Nitta Downing and I went with Art to Elitches to swim what did we do that for? We just went swimming there, I guess. What was it that Elitches had ah, swimming pool or something 'cause it was at 39th and well, that’s where Art lived. 39th and Tennyson! Yeah. And, we, ah, took some of his friends from the Boeing Aircraft and we went swimming.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: During the work week?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: During the war, yeah, it was, ah, Nitta and I went together, gosh, isn’t that funny I can’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Do you know if you made any parts for the B-29 Super Fortress?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, we made, we made parts for, of course, and a lot of things you didn’t know what you were making 'um for.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was it kind of secret?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Everything, secret.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Could you talk to your friends outside of work what you were doing?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, so every time you went to work you had to go kind of through security, nobody else could go in, you had a badge?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Ah, didn’t have a badge isn’t that funny that you mentioned it but I don’t remember havin’ a badge.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But it was secret you couldn’t tell your friends what you were doing?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: That’s right.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, yeah. Were there a lot of posters around where you worked, like "support the war, your boys are at work, at war" overseas?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah, and if you had, ah, if you had brothers in the war, you had those flags that you put in your window that said, what did they say on there?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: They weren’t stars, they were flags, is that right?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Maybe they were stars, isn’t that funny, I can’t remember; seemed like they were flags.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But back at work there were posters on the wall.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: On the wall.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Warning you to keep a secret.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Any posters like that? That the enemy is listening?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Right and always all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you were a "Rosie the Riveter"?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, what you would call.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: I think you would, did you have a "Rosie the Riveter" poster on the wall?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We may have at Art’s; but isn’t that funny I don’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now were most of the employee women at Arthur Hurt?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, there were some men and the funny part of it was the men always got, even if they ran the same machine as you did, they got paid more than you did.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now a lot of men had been drafted to go off to fight the war so were there, there were fewer men there than usual?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: There was men there, though.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Were there more women than men?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: More women.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: More women than men, okay well that makes sense.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: The women ran machines like the drills [unclear] drill presses and, ah there wasn’t many women that would run the lathes or anything. I think I was probably one of the first that started runnin’ the lathe. And, Art taught me how sharpen my own tools to set up the lathe for work, ah, I did a lot of things with Art Hurt, he taught me a lot.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: How many hours a day did you work and how many days a week did you work?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And we worked six (6) days a week ten (10) hours a day sometimes which was a long day [laughter] now that I think about it.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you were, end of the day you were pretty tired, I guess?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, ah, there for a while I worked the swing the shift, what they called the swing shift and that was, ah, from 4 o’clock to midnight would that be right? Yeah, 4 (four) 'til midnight and when I worked the swing shift we’d work different shifts because you couldn’t, you just couldn’t do that all the time. Ah, and I would work there, come home, and we’d have puzzles set up, my mother would help me with those puzzles, workin’ those puzzles until she’d say; "I think you better go to bed."

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: While you were working there did you have the patriotic spirit that you were helping to win the war with [

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, yeah] the work you did?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I definitely did and, ah, that was one thing when I went to South High School they had a scrap drive and all metal and everything they would set out on the front lawn at the high school. I’ll never forget the scrap drives and everybody brought everything you could imagine.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What, the students would bring in scrap?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Bring in scrap and then they’d pick it up in big trucks.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, I understand that, ah, Arthur Hurt sponsored a soft ball team [

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah.] for girls?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, yeah and he sponsored a soft ball team and we were we were pretty good, I must say. Ah, what was it called?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What positions did you play on the team?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I played catch, catcher and and I also played first baseman.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Were you -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Kind of ah "jack of all trades" when it came to it to the baseball team.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Were you a good hitter?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And I thought I was pretty good hitter [laughter]. Yeah, I thought I was pretty good. Ah,--

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Arthur Hurt, also sponsor a men’s team?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, he didn’t, but we won the State in the softball and then we were beat by Utah in the Regional for the Regional.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, now I assume there were not a lot of men’s baseball teams?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Because they were off to war [

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah.] and so mostly women played softball or baseball.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Most of 'um were women.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And I know there was National but you played in the State of Colorado?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, and there was, ah, down on Broadway there was what they used to call "Merchants Park" I don’t remember what it’s called now. But, we would play before the Denver Bears games which attracted a lot of people. We would, the Arthur J. Hurt would play there and we would play at Center, City Park I don’t even remember how we got there.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You had uniforms, softball uniforms?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And we had uniforms, yeah, was black and white, I’ll never forget, black and white what the heck, I don’t remember what they said.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, you mentioned in your memoirs that you actually played German POW’s?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We did play, they had, ah, ah, a German POW, we transported, that wasn’t, that wasn’t during [unclear] but we played the German POW’s and they were the nicest guys.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Where was the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And the prison camp was down on, ah, Cherry Creek, Cherry Creek and, ah, was it Broadway, or--

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So, it was actually inside the City of Denver?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was it, fences around high wire?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh they had, they had, yeah, they had barbed wire?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Barbed wire fences?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Fences around.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, did you go inside the camp to play softball?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We would go inside, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And did you talk with 'um, did you understand each other, did they speak?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, we didn’t understand that much.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: But some of 'um could speak English, but a lot of 'um couldn’t.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: How many times did you play against the German POW’s?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, and I don’t remember how many times.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But it was more than once?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah, it was more than once.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And did you win?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: You know, and at that time I don’t even remember but I know that they were thrilled to be able to do that. And, I think they were what they called 'um, trustees or somethin’ were the only ones that really got to play with you.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Oh, not all of them could?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, not all of 'um could.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you felt comfortable with them?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did they seem like the enemy or did they seem like normal human beings?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, they didn’t seem like the enemy to me, not at all.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, let’s go on to meeting and the courtship with Rosco "Mick" Amick and we’ll call him "Mick".

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, when and where did you meet Mick?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I met Mick, ah, I was babysitting his friend’s, ah, Roxie and, ah, Roxie and Milt Baldwin. And they lived just down the block from me, about, probably probably a half a block or so. And, I was babysitting them when I met Mick at that time. I’ve got a picture, I think, of me on, at Baldwin’s.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What attracted you to Mick?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I don’t know, I don’t know.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But you liked him right away.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah, I did.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: When did you start dating?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Ah, we he went into the service just right away and so we really didn’t do a lot of dating. We used to go to dancing, a lot of dancing at Lakeside Ballroom and at Trocadero, which was Elitch’s Ballroom, we did a lot of dancing there.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: How long was it from the time you met Mick until he went into the service, was it several months or weeks?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: It must have been several months, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, you did, you went dancing?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You, also, mentioned Glenn Miller came to one of those dances?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Glenn Miller was there, right.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you actually saw Glenn Miller?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And Tommy Dorsey was there.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was Glenn Miller in military uniform at that time, 'cause I know he went overseas to play for the troops?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: He wasn’t at that time when I was there, but he was when Mick was there, ah, on the, what did they call that--heck; I don’t remember what they called that.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You don’t mean leave when he came back -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did he come back on leave from the service?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh well, he’s, he in one of his letters he sent me ah was it a poster or something that said that they were there, that they that Glenn Miller and -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So Glenn Miller came to visit the troops in the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, the troops.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, the troops in the Pacific is what they did.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, but you and Mick danced to Glenn Miller back here in Denver?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, we did, yeah, later on.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Oh, after the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, after the war.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, but not during the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, okay and, ah, did Mick volunteer to join the Marines?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, he and Gaylan who was a very good friend decided to join the Marines. You know they were drafting a lot people in the Army and they didn’t want to go to the Army so they both enlisted in the Marines.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Right, I guess the Marines did not draft soldiers you had to volunteer [

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: You had to volunteer] to be a Marine. And so, in spite the risk, he wanted to join the Marines because [

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah] they were always on the front line in the, in the Pacific Theater.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, they really were in the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, when he left what were your feelings, did you feel that you would marry him when he came back from the service, did you, were you that romantically attached to Mick at that time?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I was romantically attached.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And, I thought that I would, probably marry, if he came back, you know, you always wondered.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, well did he go to training some place in California or elsewhere before he was shipped over to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah, he was at, ah what was the name, San Diego?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: San Diego?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: San Diego, yeah, he was at San Diego.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And did you get to see him before he left Denver?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My mother wouldn’t let me go [laughter] I was only 16 (sixteen) and she wouldn’t let me go.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, she let you, well you saw him off from Denver?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I saw, I, yeah, I saw him off from Denver.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But not from San Diego?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, but I couldn’t go to San Diego.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, well let’s just back-track a little bit, where were you when you learned that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Where was I?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: That was 1941 and you would have been, ah,

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I must have been in that was before I graduated.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Yes, it was.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: It was before I graduated.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Do you remember hearing it on the news and you remember what your feelings were when you heard that the Japanese -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Of course I don’t think we had, ah, maybe we had radio.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay. I assume they talked about it at school because you were in school at the time.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Somebody, yeah, they must have announced it at school, at the time. That they’d bombed Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And then about, so that was 1941 and you graduated in ah, 1943?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And, when did you meet Mick, 1943 or ’42?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, I had--don’t remember.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But any rate after Pearl Harbor; is that when Mick decided to join the Marines?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Join the Marine Corp along with Gaylan, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, I guess a lot of boys were inspired or motivated to do -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: After Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And they wanted to go they didn’t want to be drafted.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you and Mick exchanged letters during the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh, yes we wrote letters.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: How often did you write?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I would write, probably, every day and he would write whenever he could, which was not very often.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, did you save any of the letters?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Do you wish you had?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I, I wish I had now, yeah, most of 'um were just "love letter" nothin’ -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, I guess he couldn’t talk too much about what he was doing.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, no he couldn’t -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What could he write about that wasn’t censored, just kind of a love letter again, he really couldn’t talk about -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: That’s all it was, it wasn’t -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: He couldn’t say where he was located or [

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No] or what he was doing.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Or where he was going or anything.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Were some of the letters censored, where they blacked out, or cut out, did they cut out words?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, he just wouldn’t even, he didn’t write 'um.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I don’t remember 'um bein’ blacked out.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: I imagine you were worried and fearful about -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: About Mick.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And always wonderin’ and, of course, that time you didn’t hear very often, you didn’t, you didn’t get a letter from him.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, did you follow the war in the newspapers?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And the battles, especially in the Pacific, where, where Mick was.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: And so you got the newspaper every day to see what was happening?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, I don’t know if we got one every day.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I don’t remember if we got one delivered every day, ah -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, did you listen to the news on the radio about the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, you’d all just sit around the radio, you know, and hear what was going on, what they were allowed to say.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about movies? Did they have newsreels at the movies about the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: They didn’t, okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Huh-ah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay and you said they gathered around the radio to, to hear the news about the war. Did you ever hear FDR in one of his "fireside chats" during the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yes, one time we did maybe more once but FDR was a very favorite of ours. I think he was of a lot of people.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Yea, so you do remember listening to him on the radio?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Un-huh.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Tell me about rationing, what was rationed during the war years?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, what I remember is meat ah, butter, things like that, ah what else was rationed?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about gasoline and cars and tires?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And gasoline, of course, you, you would get so many gallon and my dad worked just down, down town and there would be, ah, there would be two (2) or three (3) of 'um riding in one car, you know, so you could use your gasoline stamps for several of 'um.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: I remember in your memoirs you talk about, I don’t know if it was your Dad or someone else who would get a lot of flat tires and he’d have to repair the tires 'cause you couldn’t buy new ones.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh yeah, my Dad did. [laughter] I even remember and once in a while we’d take a ride on Sunday up to the hills and he would, you’d never go anywhere that you wouldn’t have a flat tire. You know, they had those bladders in the tires and you and you scraped 'um off and they put, ah, rubber, or patches on 'um, I guess is what they called 'um and then pump up the tire. Get in and away we’d go for a little while.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you dad wasn’t able to buy any new tires while the war was going on?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, not at all so you really made do.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Where did you get your ration stamps from, did they mail them to you or did you go to the post office to pick them up?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I, you know, what did we do? They must of mailed 'um to us, I don’t remember goin’ to get any?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: You’d get them once a week or once a month, or?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Somethin’ like that, once a week, probably, but of course there was 7 (seven) of us kids so, you know we, at that time, we probably got a few more grocery stamps and things than most people but I don’t remember the stamps, isn’t that funny, I thought that I’d never forget that.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, I believe your brothers Hal and Bob also served in the military.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Could you tell us about where they were?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Hal was in the Army and he was the oldest in the Army and he was fightin’ the Germans over in Germany he was at the battle, what they called "The Battle of the Bulge" which was one of the worst battles in Germany.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did he write home about his experiences?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, he couldn’t.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Again, it was censored.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Censored, everything was censored, you don’t, you didn’t write about any of that.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Do you know if he was on the front lines during the "Battle of the Bulge"?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We knew he was up there somewhere but didn’t know where.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, and I know, ah, what the, see Hal started at Italy, I think he went up Italy and then went on up to Germany and fought. But "The Battle of the Bulge" was at Germany and, ah -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did he stay in Europe until the war was over, he didn’t come home on leave, I guess, he stayed there.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, he didn’t get leave [laughter], at all.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: What about your other brother, what was his name?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Bob.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Bob, where did he serve?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Bob was in the, ah, Merchant Marines, which, which protected the mostly the, ah, clear up to Alaska. Mostly the, what do I want to call it, Pacific what was it, the Pacific, ah goin’ up to Alaska? But he was in the Merchant Marines.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did he write letters home?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And he would write, too, but not, like I say everything was censored so you didn’t get the -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So, I assume, he wrote the letters to his mother, not to you, or to the whole family?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, yeah, to the family, not to his mother, probably.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, let’s go on to the end of World War II, how did you hear about the end of the war in Europe, did you hear about it in school, oh, you were out of school by then. Did you hear it on the radio?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: My brother, we had it on the radio 'cause, I’ll never forget, we lived on Kalamath Street, my brother was home on leave -

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: From Europe, which brother?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: From, no, not the one in Europe the one on the coast.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, in the Merchant Marines.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Merchant Marines and he was home on leave and we lived, Kalamath Street was the thorough street that most everybody took from say downtown Denver to South Denver, there. And, I’ll never forget when the war was over, Daddy bought a bottle and every car that came down Kalamath Street, cause that’s the only way they had goin’ down to South Denver there where we lived would stop and everybody have a drink. And my brother, Bob, who doesn’t drink at all now, at that time got polluted along with my dad.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now was this after the war in Europe ended or after the war in Japan, in the Pacific ended?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Of Europe.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Europe, yeah, yeah, and, ah

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: How did you celebrate the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Takin’ care of my brother and my dad who was both so polluted [laughter] I think that’s all we did my mother and us girls were just takin’ care of Daddy.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well; how did you hear about the end of the war in the Pacific about the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, you remember the days that that happened, did they, they reported on the radio, I assume.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: It was on radio and, but I was workin’ at the machine shop at the time.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: That’s right you were still working even after the war, you worked until 19 -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, that was before I got sick.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now, when the boys came home from the war, from the Pacific or from Europe they all, they kind of bumped a lot of the women out of the war plants. But you were able to keep your job?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I did keep my job.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you, a lot of ladies that you worked with lose their job?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Some of the ladies were still there, I can remember Mary Hamilton; she lived right there on Kalamath where I did and she worked, she did the drill presses.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So if you had some special abilities they kept you?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: They kept you.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But a lot of the other women, they were replaced.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Well, they glad just to get out of there.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: I guess they were.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, really.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay, the war is over and, ah, when did you get married?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: We got married February 15th and we chose the 15th because we had 3 (three) days off with the 15th.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Was that 1946?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: ’46, was it?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: See Mick didn’t come back from the Pacific -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yeah, ’46, it must have been.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Until like September of 1945 and then you got married in September -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: February.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Februray of ’50 -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: February.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: February of ’46?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: 15th of ’46.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: At Redeemer Luthern Church, I’ll never forget it. On Mississippi and where was it? I don’t remember now.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Where did you and Mick live after you were married?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And he wasn’t even workin’ at the time we were married. I was and he wasn’t but he got a job as ah, where did he get that first job? Guess at Martin Marrietta, did he, no--

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Where did you work, now how long did you continue working for Arthur Hurt, you stayed there for a number of years?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, I stayed there for a number of years, until I got sick and then I was off because I had a brain tumor and--

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So you were out of work for some time?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I was out of work for some time and, of course, when I got back Art hired me again at the machine shop and I worked upstairs, I remember, doing what, what did I do up there?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Now I don’t assume you weren’t making parts for Boeing Aircraft -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Anymore, no military.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No, not any more.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: No more war time effort?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: No more war time.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: But you eventually left Arthur Hurt and you worked somewhere else? You became a realtor, I believe?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Oh, well, yeah I was a realtor when I came back, we moved out to Castle Rock.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: 'Cause we lived in Denver at that time and then we moved to Castle Rock oh, we lived at Castle Rock when I still worked at Art’s, didn’t we?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: That was a long commute.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Yes I did, too funny.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Anything you’d like tell us about your children during their growing-up years?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I had David and Jim and David was, ah, oh always kind of the mild-mannered one. Jim was a little bit, ah, what do I say, Jim was independent more or less. Ah,

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well is there anything else you’d -

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: David went to college at Northern, no CSU at CSU, David went college. But Jim didn’t want to go to college, he--

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: So how long were you a realtor, several years?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: I was a realtor several years, yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Did you enjoy that?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: And I did enjoy it, yeah, I really enjoyed it and I--I knew a lot of, as a matter of fact I just met a lady that I had known down in Perry Park which was when I was realtor and Perry Park was just beginning to develop at that time. Perry Park and then most of Castle Rock area I worked with Metro Brokers.

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well, let’s see, let’s we’re going to close pretty soon now. Is there anything you’d like to tell us about your experiences on the home front during WWII, anything else that we can talk about?

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: You know, at the present time, I can’t. I remember I have, ah, what, your annual, you know where my annual is--do you have it?

sp.speaker: Larry Adams
sp.p: Well that’s okay, let’s close. I want to thank you for sharing your story; it will be archived at the Library of Congress and at the Douglas County History Research Center for use by future generations to help them understand what it was like experiencing the war years. Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Margaret Amick
sp.p: Thank you. [END OF INTERVIEW]
